summary: This standards-track RFC describes how to carry VP8 video, a video codec, inside RTP packets. It covers uses from low-bitrate peer-to-peer calls to high-bitrate video conferences.

plainLanguage.summary: A video is chopped into small packets so it can travel over the internet. This explains how to cut up and label VP8 video so the other side can put it back together.

subtitle: How to chop VP8 video into RTP packets so receivers can cope with loss and servers can drop what they must.

tldr.problem: VP8 video frames are larger than a packet and are made of parts of differing importance, so sending them over RTP needs rules for splitting, labelling and recovering from loss.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP packet starts with a VP8 payload descriptor that marks partition starts, non-reference frames, picture numbers and temporal layers. The first packet of a frame also carries the VP8 payload header, and RTCP feedback (RPSI and SLI) helps the sender recover.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can conceal loss per partition, and network elements can discard non-reference frames. It is a Proposed Standard and nothing in the unit metadata says it has been replaced.

today: RFC 7741 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2016. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 7741 describes how to carry video encoded with the VP8 codec (RFC 6386) in RTP. It is meant for both peer-to-peer use and video conferencing.

VP8 splits each frame into square blocks called macroblocks. An encoded frame has two or more partitions. The first holds prediction modes and motion vectors for all macroblocks. The rest hold the quantized transform coefficients for the residuals, and there can be 1, 2, 4 or 8 of these depending on encoder settings.

The payload format makes several features possible: using partition boundaries to improve loss robustness and concealment, temporal scalability, advanced use of reference frames for error recovery, and marking frames that no other frame depends on, so a server or media-aware network element can discard them if needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A video frame is like a jigsaw picture made of a few big chunks. This RFC says how to pack those chunks into envelopes so a missing envelope doesn't ruin the whole picture.

sections.title: How VP8 Frames Behave
sections.content:
VP8 uses three reference frames for interframe prediction: the previous frame, the golden frame and the altref frame. Every key frame is automatically golden and altref, and any interframe may replace the most recent golden or altref frame. These extra references can increase tolerance to dropped frames. By setting up the reference hierarchy suitably, up to five temporal layers can be encoded. That setup is out of scope for the RFC.

The first partition can be decoded without the others, and the later partitions may still be useful if part of a frame is lost. The RFC therefore RECOMMENDS that the sender put each data partition in its own packet or packets. This helps decoder-side error concealment. The sender may instead aggregate the partitions into one stream and split it without regard to boundaries. The receiver then uses the length information in the first partition to find the partitions.

The use of RTP/AVPF (RFC 4585) is RECOMMENDED so that losses can be handled. All integer fields are unsigned and in network octet order.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a picture where the outline arrives first and the colouring comes in later pieces. If a colouring piece is lost you can still see the outline, so it helps to send the pieces in separate envelopes.

sections.title: RTP Header and VP8 Payload Descriptor
sections.content:
The RTP fixed header is used as in RFC 3550, with three details. The marker bit (M) MUST be set on the very last packet of each encoded frame. The payload type is assigned outside this document. The timestamp tells when the frame was sampled, with a 90 kHz clock, so a delta of 1 represents 1/90,000 of a second.

After the RTP header comes the VP8 payload descriptor. Its mandatory first octet has these bits:

  • X: extended control bits follow. If 0, all optional fields must be omitted.
  • N: non-reference frame. When 1, the frame can be discarded without affecting any other frame. If its reference status is unknown, set it to 0.
  • S: start of a VP8 partition. It MUST be 1 for the first packet of every frame.
  • PID: partition index, with the first partition labelled 0. It cannot be larger than 7.

When X is 1, a second octet carries the flags I, L, T and K, which say which optional fields follow: PictureID, TL0PICIDX and the TID/Y/KEYIDX octet. The PictureID is a running frame index of 7 or 15 bits, chosen by the sender with the M flag. TL0PICIDX is an 8-bit index for temporal base layer frames. TID is a 2-bit temporal layer number, Y is a layer sync bit, and KEYIDX is a 5-bit key frame index.
sections.plainLanguage: Every envelope gets a small sticker. The sticker says whether this envelope starts a new chunk, whether it is safe to throw away, and which picture number it belongs to.

sections.title: Payload Header, Aggregation and Fragmentation
sections.content:
The start of an encoded VP8 frame, the uncompressed data chunk of RFC 6386, doubles as the VP8 payload header. It is 3 octets for interframes and 10 octets for key frames, and the first 3 octets are common to both. It appears only in packets with S equal to 1 and PID equal to 0. A packetizer needs access to the P bit, where 0 means a key frame and 1 means an interframe. The other fields are not modified.

A packetizer MAY ignore partition boundaries, in which case PID may stay 0 in every packet and S must be 1 only in the first. Then one packet can hold a fragment of a partition, a complete partition or an aggregate of both, and partitions MUST be aggregated in decoding order. In every case a packet's payload MUST contain data from only one video frame, and the last packet of the frame has the M bit set.

The RFC gives example algorithms. To rebuild a frame, collect all packets with the same RTP timestamp, order them by sequence number, send a NACK if any are missing, and treat the frame as complete when there are no gaps, the first packet has S=1 with partition 0, and the last packet has the marker bit. A partition-level algorithm abandons any partition with a detected loss, sends the complete ones to the decoder, and discards the frame if none is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: Each frame is sent in envelopes that never mix two frames. The last envelope for a frame is stamped with a special mark, so the receiver knows the frame is finished.

sections.title: Recovering from Loss with RPSI and SLI
sections.content:
The optional PictureID exists mainly so that two RTCP feedback messages from RFC 4585 can be used. RPSI (reference picture selection indication) lets the receiver acknowledge that it correctly decoded a golden or altref frame. Its body is simply the PictureID of that frame. SLI (slice loss indication) tells the sender that part of a frame was lost or corrupted. It carries the first lost macroblock address, the number of lost blocks and the six least significant bits of the PictureID.

The RFC illustrates a scheme in which the golden and altref frames are updated alternately, and the encoder will not update the altref until the last golden frame has been acknowledged with RPSI. When an SLI arrives, the sender encodes the next frame with reference to the established reference, so the decoder state is restored.

The scheme tolerates feedback loss. If an RPSI is lost, the sender later tries the update again without releasing the established reference. If an SLI is lost, the receiver can keep sending SLI messages, within the RTCP timing limits, for as long as the picture is corrupted.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver sends back tiny notes: "I got picture 100 fine" or "picture 100 is broken." The sender then builds the next picture from the last one it knows the receiver has.

sections.title: Media Type and SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type video/VP8. It has no required parameters and two optional ones that describe a receiver's limits: max-fr, the maximum frame rate in frames per second, and max-fs, the maximum frame size in macroblocks. If an implementation is willing to receive media, both parameters MUST be provided. A frame fits if its width and height in macroblocks are less than int(sqrt(max-fs * 8)). For example, a max-fs of 1200, enough for 640x480, supports widths and heights up to 1552 pixels (97 macroblocks).

In SDP the media name MUST be video, the encoding name MUST be VP8 and the clock rate MUST be 90000. A receiver MUST ignore any fmtp parameter this memo does not define. The macroblock size used for these limits is 16x16 pixels.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a video call, each side says how big and how fast a picture it can handle, a bit like telling a friend the biggest box you can carry.

sections.title: Security and Congestion Control
sections.content:
The packets are subject to the security considerations of RTP (RFC 3550) and of whichever RTP profile is used. Choosing the security mechanism is up to whoever uses RTP, and applications SHOULD use one or more appropriate strong mechanisms. The payload format itself has no significant extra receiver-side processing cost, so it is unlikely to cause a denial-of-service problem from pathological data, and it contains no active content.

Congestion control for RTP SHALL be used as in RFC 3550 and the applicable profile, for instance RFC 3551. Media-aware network elements MAY use the payload descriptor to spot non-reference frames and discard them to reduce congestion. This cannot be done if the stream is encrypted, because the non-reference marker is encrypted too.
sections.plainLanguage: The video envelopes need the same locks as any other RTP traffic. If the road is jammed, a helper can toss out the envelopes marked safe to drop, but only if it can read the stickers, which it cannot when they are locked inside encryption.
